misconceptions.believed: That STRETCH -- how far below their mastery a player's difficulty sits -- was the parameter controlling the success rate, and would need tuning to land the band. I wrote it with a comment calling it 'the dial to turn if the simulated band comes out wrong'.
misconceptions.revealed_by: Sweeping it, because writing that comment obliged me to check it. Success moves from 70% at zero offset to 74% at three times the shipped value -- nearly flat across the whole plausible range.
misconceptions.corrected_to: The loop is self-correcting: lowering difficulty raises the observed result, which raises mastery, which raises difficulty back, so the offset cancels itself out. The equilibrium success rate is set by the observation weights in mastery.py -- accuracy 0.5, functional 0.3, first-try 0.2 -- not by anything in the policy. STRETCH expresses an intent rather than controlling an outcome, and the module and trajectory now both say so.
misconceptions.generalisable_lesson: In a feedback loop, a parameter's local effect is not its effect. I reasoned about STRETCH one step at a time -- lower difficulty, higher success -- and stopped before the step where mastery follows difficulty back up. Sweeping a parameter is cheap; predicting it is where the error is.

misconceptions.believed: That the 60-90% success band could be met for all four simulated players, and that failing to would mean the policy needed work.
misconceptions.revealed_by: Measuring. Always-correct and always-naive succeed 100% of the time at every one of 40 seeds.
misconceptions.corrected_to: No difficulty policy can change that, because W2's dial scales how much work an input demands rather than whether the answer is right -- which is the design, and is why a level's hand-written edge cases survive every difficulty. A correct solution passes at every input size, so a player who always writes one is unreachable; 'naive' in this codebase means O(n^2) and right, so it lands in the same place. Criterion 3 is met for the two players who can fail and is structurally unmeetable for the two who cannot. N7 forbids re-cutting it, so it stands and Q89 carries the finding.
misconceptions.generalisable_lesson: The near-miss is the part worth keeping. My first simulation used a step function (cleared = reach >= 0.5) to avoid seed dependence, which made every player succeed 100% -- including the plateaued one -- and would have looked like the same structural finding while actually being my model being wrong. It also scored Functional as efficiency x (1 - 0.3*difficulty), which penalised a perfect player, when the real axis is measured against the reference running the same variant and so gives a perfect solution 100 at any size. A simulation is a model, and one that produces a striking result is the one to distrust first: keeping the player's latent skill invisible stops the policy cheating, but nothing stops the model being wrong except checking that each of its terms has the property the real thing has.

decisions.decision: The reason is produced with the decision, in the same object
alternatives: Generate explanations in W7 from the stored numbers
decisions.rationale: Criterion 4 says 'no hidden state'. Two code paths that can disagree, one of which the player sees, is exactly that.

decisions.decision: Mastery and habits are used one at a time and always named, never blended
alternatives: A weighted average of the two, with the habit term falling off as observations accumulate
decisions.rationale: The blend is what exit criterion 8 forbids and what T4's third hazard calls the most tempting wrong simplification. Naming the source lets the player judge the guess.

decisions.decision: The habits prior is bounded at +-0.15
alternatives: Let familiarity drive the full difficulty range
decisions.rationale: Habits are a guess about performance, not a measurement of it. The worst a wrong prior may do is hand someone a slightly roomier or tighter first run.

decisions.decision: reference_benchmark takes the difficulty, and it is part of the cache key
alternatives: Benchmark at the default and compare against it
decisions.rationale: Otherwise the Functional axis divides a player's ops by a denominator measured on a smaller input, and punishes them for a size the game chose.

decisions.decision: The band is asserted pooled over 20 seeds rather than on one run
alternatives: Assert a single 50-level run at a fixed seed
decisions.rationale: A single run has a standard error of about 6 points and sits two points from the band edge. That test passes today and fails on a Tuesday.

decisions.decision: Criterion 3 stands as written, with the finding recorded against it
alternatives: Re-cut it to cover only players who can fail
Drop the two players from the instrument check
decisions.rationale: N7. An exit criterion edited to match what was built destroys the only honest signal a trajectory has.

friction.description: none - both findings came from measuring things I had written down as assumptions, which is the cheap direction.

handoff.state: T4 W1-W4 LANDED. A player's profile now chooses their variant's difficulty, with the reason attached, and the reference is benchmarked on the same variant. Exit criteria 1, 2, 4 and 5 are verified; 3 is verified for the two simulated players who can fail and is structurally unmeetable for the two who cannot (Q89). 1165 tests green unpinned, 1141 pinned, verify clean on 54 reference runs.
handoff.next_action: T4 W5, drill injection on the weakest tag. It is also the intended answer to Q88: three tags have exactly one level each and can never reach the confidence threshold from ordinary play, so drills are what would give them evidence.

Exit criterion 3's band cannot hold for a player who always writes correct code. W2's difficulty scales work rather than correctness, so a correct solution passes at every size, by design. Either 'success' means something other than 'cleared' for a scored game (three stars? a score threshold?), or the criterion needs a player who can actually fail. Which?
